nutrient-calories-role: Your body needs calories to do things. Your calorie reserve is refilled over time by macro-nutrients such as Fats, Protein, and Carbs. If your calorie reserve reaches zero, your body will begin to starve.
nutrient-protein-role: Protein is needed to build and maintain muscle mass. It is processed and absorbed very differently by your body, and a specific amount must be ingested every 24hrs to meet your goals. Excess protein cannot be absorbed and provides no benefit. Protein provides 4kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-carbohydrate-role: Carbs make up the majority of most diets. They are quickly processed by your body into Calories, but cannot be stored for very long and have quickly diminishing returns if eaten too quickly. Carbs provide 4kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-fat-role: Fats are much slower to process but provide your body with more consistent energy over time. You can store a lot more fats in your reserve than any other macro-nutrient. Fats provide 9kcal per gram (g) when absorbed.
nutrient-fiber-role: Fiber keeps your digestion moving and confers absorption rate buffs to each of your macro-nutrients. Keep your daily Fiber intake above 70% to get the best benefits.
nutrient-vitaminK-role: Lets blood clot and wounds close.

guide-overview-text:
Eating Well
A full stomach is not the same as a good diet

Every food now carries real-world nutrition: calories, carbs, fats, protein and fiber, four fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K), vitamin C, the B vitamins, and three minerals (calcium, iron and potassium). Hold a food to see what one portion of it contains, or hold a bowl or pie to see what one serving contains. Amounts are shown in grams and kcal, and in mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals.

Your body keeps track of each of these fourteen nutrients. Open the character screen (characterdialog) to see them under Nutritional Reserves, where the five food group bars used to be. Each block on a bar is one day's worth. Hovering over a bar shows how much you have, how long it will last and what the nutrient does. Typing /nutrition in chat lists them all.

Fullness and Calories
Fullness is how much your stomach holds, out of 300. It decides how much more you can eat, and it empties within 6 hours whatever you do. What keeps you alive is your calorie reserve, shown by the bar next to your hotbar. It holds about a week of hard work. Digestion fills it and activity burns it, and when it runs dry you start to starve. The other reserves show whether what you eat is any good. A stomach full of bread will keep you going, but it won't keep your vitamin C up.

While nutrient tracking is turned on, the five vanilla food group bars and the bonus health they give are switched off completely. Only one nutrition system can run at a time. Toggling off Complex Nutrition Tracking in the mod settings will adjust your nutrition values to their vanilla equivalents. Be warned that switching Complex Nutrition Tracking back on will set your nutrient values back to the state they were in before the system was toggled off.

For now, calories and fiber are the only nutrients with an effect in game. The effects of a good or poor diet will arrive in a later version.

Read on: Digestion, Nutrient Reserves, How Food Is Counted and The Fourteen Nutrients.
guide-reserves-text:
Nutrient Reserves
Measured in days

Reserves are shown as amounts: kcal for calories, grams for carbs, fats, protein and fiber, and mg or mcg for vitamins and minerals. The B vitamins are a mix of six, so they are shown as a percentage of a day's need. Each reserve also tells you how many days it would last if you stopped eating that nutrient altogether, and each block on its bar is one day.

To see every amount as a percentage of a day's need instead, tooltips included, set DisplayUnits to "percent" in ModConfig/complexnutrition.json.

Daily Needs
An active day burns about 2,800 kcal. You need at least 64 g of protein every 24 hours, and your body can use up to 128 g. Fiber's daily need is 30 g. Carbs and fats have no daily need of their own, because your body simply turns them into calories. Vitamins and minerals use the adult daily values printed on real food labels: vitamin A 900 mcg, vitamin D 20 mcg, vitamin E 15 mg, vitamin K 120 mcg, vitamin C 90 mg, calcium 1,300 mg, iron 18 mg and potassium 4,700 mg.

Using It Up
Vitamins, minerals and fiber each use up one day's worth per in-game day, whether you are awake or asleep. Calories burn with activity. Standing still burns about 700 kcal a day and moving all day burns about 2,800. Sprinting, the cold and anything else that raises your hunger rate burns more. Carbs, fats and protein are not stored in the same way. They sit in your gut until they are digested into calories, and the Stats panel shows how much is still being digested. Nothing is used up in creative mode or while you are logged out.

How Much the Body Can Store
• Calories: up to 7 active days (19,600 kcal), which is a store of body fat. A new character starts with 5 days' worth on a Normal start. The Starting Calories setting, on the Complex Nutrition tab when you create a world, can give a new character anything from a full tank down to almost nothing.
• Vitamins A, D, E and K: up to 25 days (22,500 mcg of vitamin A, for example). A new character starts with two weeks' worth, so running low takes a long time, and so does recovering.
• Calcium, iron and potassium: up to 10 days (180 mg of iron, for example). A new character starts with a week's worth.
• Vitamin C, the B vitamins and fiber: up to 2 days (180 mg of vitamin C, for example). A new character starts with one day's worth, so these are the first to run low.

Anything eaten past a full store is lost.

See also: Digestion and How Food Is Counted.
guide-counting-title: Complex Nutrition: How Food Is Counted
guide-counting-text:
How Food Is Counted
Every ingredient counts

Single Foods
Each food has the weight of a real-world portion, and its nutrition comes from real food data for that weight. Spoiling food gives less fullness and fewer nutrients in the same measure, and rot gives nothing. How full a food makes you depends on its weight, not its calories (see Digestion).

Meals
A serving from the cooking pot counts as the sum of its ingredients. Cooking makes food easier to digest but destroys some vitamins. A cooked meal gives about 20% more carbs and 10% more protein than its raw ingredients, so more calories, but only half the vitamin C and three quarters of the B vitamins. Crock pot contents are simply preserved and receive no nutritional losses or buffs from storage.

Pies and Bread
A pie's calories and nutrients include the values from both its filling and its crust. A slice is a quarter of the pie's total value. Charred or part-baked pies and bread lose a lot of their nutrition.

Drinks
Drinks provide their full nutritional benefit but at half the fullness rate, enabling you to take in a lot more. They are an excellent source and store of most vitamins. A sip a day keeps the scurvy away!

Large Meals
Your body can only take in so much of each nutrient at once. Carbs, fats and protein give fewer calories once you have digested a lot of them in a short time (see Digestion). Fiber, vitamins and minerals work in a similar way. Everything you eat within an hour of your last food is added together, and up to a day and a half's worth of each nutrient is taken in fully. Past that, each extra day's worth only adds about two thirds of a day to your reserve. Spreading rich foods out and eating a mix of them works better than one big feast.

Mushrooms
Every mushroom species has its own nutrient profile. All of them are light and low in calories, but some are worth the hunt. Morels are rich in iron, and chanterelles and morels both carry vitamin D. Woody brackets such as reishi and tinder hoof are mostly fiber. Each mushroom weighs about what a real one would. Mushrooms that grow in clusters give you several at once, so a patch of morels or liberty caps gives four to eight small mushrooms, while a king bolete or an oyster mushroom gives one big one. Poisonous species still have their nutrients, and they will still poison you.

Foods from Other Mods
Foods without nutrition data of their own are estimated from their food group and vanilla satiety. Full support for other mods is planned, and modders can add their nutrient profiles using the template included with this mod's release files. Complex Nutrition will automatically import these when loading the world.

See also: The Fourteen Nutrients.
guide-digestion-text:
Digestion
From stomach to calorie reserve

Fullness
Your stomach holds 300 fullness, which is about a kilogram of food. Every food fills you by its weight: an apple fills 54, a loaf of bread 54 and a whole cabbage 270. Meals, pies and anything cooked, baked, smoked or cured fill you 20% less, so cooking lets you eat more at once. Drinks fill you half as much as their weight would. Fullness drains by 50 every hour, whatever you are doing, so a full stomach is empty in 6 hours. It only decides whether you can eat. Food that doesn't fit has to wait, and an empty stomach does you no harm.

The Gut
Whatever you eat goes into your gut and is digested over the next few hours. Each food is digested evenly over its own time:
• Carbs (not counting their fiber) take about 3 hours. Your gut holds up to 500 g at a time.
• Protein takes about 6 hours. Your gut holds up to 200 g at a time.
• Fats take about 24 hours. Your gut holds up to 240 g at a time.

Anything eaten past a full gut passes straight through and is wasted.

Your body can only make good use of so much of each macro-nutrient at once, so eating more than that gives diminishing returns. Every gram you digest counts towards a running total. Once that total passes a certain amount, each extra gram gives you fewer calories than the last:
• Carbs: past 300 g digested in 12 hours.
• Fats: past 70 g digested in 24 hours.
• Protein: past 65 g digested in 24 hours, falling to nothing at 128 g. Protein past 128 g in a day gives no calories and no benefit at all.

The totals fall again as the hours pass, so spreading your meals across the day works better than one big feast.

Calories
Digestion is the only thing that fills your calorie reserve. Each gram of carbs or protein gives 4 kcal and each gram of fats gives 9 kcal. The reserve holds 7 active days and activity burns it. The bar next to your hotbar shows it, one block per day, and flashes when it falls below a tenth. When it is empty you starve, losing health until you eat. After dying you come back with at least a day's worth.

Fiber
When your fiber reserve is at 70% of a day's need or more, digestion runs faster: fats by 30%, protein by 20% and carbs by 10%. The bonus shrinks as the reserve runs down. In real life fiber tends to slow digestion down a little, but here it is a reward for eating your greens.

What This Means
A stomach full of stew gives about 1,000 kcal, a stomach full of bread over 3,000, and a stomach full of mushrooms very little. Fruit and vegetables alone won't carry a hard-working day, so add meat, grain, bread or cheese.

See also: Nutrient Reserves and How Food Is Counted.
guide-nutrients-text:
The Fourteen Nutrients
What they do and where to find them

Calories and fiber are the only nutrients with an effect on your character so far, and carbs, fats and protein are what your body makes calories from. Every other nutrient will get its own effect in a later version, even if a small one. Until then, its entry below says In game: planned.

Calories: your body needs calories to do things. Your calorie reserve is refilled over time by macro-nutrients such as carbs, fats and protein. If it reaches zero, your body will begin to starve. The richest foods are fat, butter, honey, nuts and bread. In game: an empty reserve starves you.
Carbs: carbs make up the majority of most diets. They are quickly turned into calories, but they can't be stored for very long and have quickly diminishing returns if you eat too much of them too quickly. Carbs give 4 kcal per gram once absorbed. Grains, bread, honey and cassava. In game: digested into calories within about 3 hours.
Fats: fats are much slower to process, but they give your body more consistent energy over time. You can store a lot more fats than any other macro-nutrient. Fats give 9 kcal per gram once absorbed, and they are needed to take in vitamins A, D, E and K. Animal fat, butter, walnuts, peanuts, cheese and sunflower seeds. In game: digested into calories over about 24 hours.
Protein: protein is needed to build and maintain muscle mass. Your body processes and absorbs it very differently from carbs and fats, and you need to eat a certain amount of it every 24 hours. Excess protein can't be absorbed and gives no benefit. Protein gives 4 kcal per gram once absorbed. Meat, fish, cheese, soybeans and peanuts. In game: digested into calories within about 6 hours. Muscle is planned.
Fiber: fiber keeps your digestion moving and speeds up how quickly each of your macro-nutrients is absorbed. Keep your fiber reserve above 70% to get the best benefit. Flax, rye, soybeans, peanuts and berries. In game: speeds up digestion.
Vitamin C: healing, and healthy gums. Sailors who went without it got scurvy. Blackcurrants, cloudberries, bell peppers, strawberries and oranges. Cooking destroys some of it. In game: planned.
B vitamins: they turn food into energy. Meat, fish, soybeans, peanuts and sunflower seeds. In game: planned.
Vitamin A: eyesight and skin. Carrots, butter, pumpkin and cheese. In game: planned.
Vitamin D: strong bones, together with calcium. Smoked and cured fish, chanterelles, morels and eggs. In game: planned.
Vitamin E: protects the body's cells. Sunflower seeds, peanuts and olives. In game: planned.
Vitamin K: lets blood clot and wounds close. Cabbage, fennel, soybeans, parsnips, blackberries and blueberries. In game: planned.
Calcium: bones and teeth. Cheese, soybeans, milk and flax. In game: planned.
Iron: carries oxygen in the blood. Soybeans, morels, bushmeat, olives and amaranth. In game: planned.
Potassium: keeps muscles and nerves working. Soybeans, fish, cattail and papyrus roots, and peanuts. In game: planned.

See also: Nutrient Reserves.
